growth_story.headline: Costa Rica's income per person has grown a steady 2.7 percent a year since 1990; lately free trade zone exports lead while the rest of the economy lags.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, Costa Rica's income per person has grown at about 2.7 percent a year with no lasting shift in pace, and in 2025 it reached its highest level yet. That record followed the debt crisis of the early 1980s, when income per person fell 9.8 percent in 1982. Afterwards the country opened to trade, and from the late 1990s it drew high-tech foreign firms such as Intel, which brought in more foreign investment. Downturns since then have been short: income per person fell 2.2 percent in 2009 and 4.8 percent in 2020, then grew 7.7 percent in 2021. The pace has barely changed from one decade to the next, at 3.1 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 3.0 percent over 2016–2025. The World Bank links recent strength to exports of medical devices and services, and the IMF finds growth outside the free trade zones much slower than inside them.

threads.title: Opening up after the debt crisis
threads.text: After the debt crisis of the early 1980s, Costa Rica opened its economy to trade. From the late 1990s it went after high-tech foreign firms such as Intel. The World Bank says this also helped create a dual economy: a strong export sector beside smaller firms that could not keep up.

citations.title: Unleashing Central America's Growth Potential: Costa Rica
citations.quote: The commercial opening expanded in the 1980s as a way to recover from the debt crisis.

citations.title: Unleashing Central America's Growth Potential: Costa Rica
citations.quote: During the second half of the 1990s, Costa Rica began a more aggressive policy of attracting investments from high-tech companies such as Intel

citations.title: Unleashing Central America's Growth Potential: Costa Rica
citations.quote: this process also contributed to creating a dual economy, with a dynamic and competitive export sector and another less-competitive sector

threads.title: Two economies, two speeds
threads.text: Exports of medical devices and business services now outweigh the older farm and tourism exports. In 2025 the IMF found that the free trade zones grew far faster than the rest of the economy, so growth created fewer jobs and spread less to local firms.

citations.title: Costa Rica: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: This has been particularly true for advanced manufacturing (notably medical devices) and business services, which now exceed the more traditional agricultural and tourism exports.

citations.title: Costa Rica: Staff Report for the 2026 Article IV Consultation and Review under the Flexible Credit Line Arrangement—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: Growth outside of the FTZs has been more restrained (3 percent y/y in 2025 compared with 12.7 percent y/y for the FTZs)

citations.title: Costa Rica: Staff Report for the 2026 Article IV Consultation and Review under the Flexible Credit Line Arrangement—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: In this context, growth is less employment-intensive and has limited spillovers to the domestic economy.

threads.title: Short, sharp shocks
threads.text: Downturns since 1990 have been brief. Income per person fell 2.2 percent in 2009 and quickly recovered, and after a 4.8 percent fall in 2020 it grew 7.7 percent in 2021, the start of the fast run the IMF describes.

citations.title: Unleashing Central America's Growth Potential: Costa Rica
citations.quote: During the 2009 global crisis, real GDP per capita contracted by 2.3 percent, but quickly returned to its upward trajectory

citations.title: Costa Rica: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: Growth has averaged over 5 percent since 2021, outpacing regional peers and contributing to improvements in social indicators.

threads.title: Fiscal repair under a rule
threads.text: In much of the 2010s the government ran the largest budget deficit in Central America. The IMF credits strict adherence to a fiscal rule with lowering borrowing costs, and says lower public spending helped hold back growth outside the free trade zones in 2025.

citations.title: Unleashing Central America's Growth Potential: Costa Rica
citations.quote: Costa Rica has the largest general budget deficit in Central America, averaging 5.4 percent of GDP in 2010-2017

citations.title: Costa Rica: Staff Report for the 2026 Article IV Consultation and Review under the Flexible Credit Line Arrangement—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: Strong growth, combined with strict adherence to the fiscal rule, lowered sovereign spreads and cuts in the policy rate have supported activity.

citations.title: Costa Rica: Staff Report for the 2026 Article IV Consultation and Review under the Flexible Credit Line Arrangement—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: in part due to a reduction in fiscal outlays on goods, services, and transfers.

threads.text: Homicide rates have been relatively high for the past three years, linked to organized crime and drug trafficking. The IMF says this has already hurt tourism and spending at home.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 income per person grew 4.1 percent and reached a new high, driven by exports of medical devices and services. Since March 2026 the IMF has expected slower growth, pointing to US tariffs, the closure of several key businesses in the free trade zones and, by June, higher oil prices.

citations.title: Costa Rica (country overview)
citations.quote: Growth accelerated to 4.6 percent in 2025, driven by exports, particularly medical devices and services.

citations.title: Costa Rica: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: the closure of several key businesses operating in the free trade zones

citations.title: Costa Rica: Staff Report for the 2026 Article IV Consultation and Review under the Flexible Credit Line Arrangement—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Costa Rica
citations.quote: Growth is projected to moderate to 3.6 percent in 2026, as headwinds from higher oil prices and tariffs more-than-offset rising investment and strong export performance.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a boom, with fast growth since 2021 and output in the free trade zones surging in 2025. The data show something steadier. Income per person grew 3.0 percent a year over 2016–2025, no faster than the 3.1 percent of 2006–2015, and part of the recent speed made up for the 4.8 percent fall in 2020. The IMF itself finds growth outside the zones much slower than the headline.
